decorative: Front cover: "HISTORY — Grade-VI, Test Edition", based on Single National Curriculum 2022, with a large "6", an ancient village scene, a sunset with a minaret, and ancient stone columns; KPTBB logo.
Advertisement page of the website that scanned the book (awazeinqilab.com). Not part of the textbook; not reproduced.
Two quotations in floral frames.
Inner title page: "HISTORY — Grade-VI", Based on Single National Curriculum 2022, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Textbook Board, Peshawar.

issues: Names are read from OCR of a small-print page ("Zulfigar Ali S, GHs maila, Swab" read as Zulfiqar Ali, SS, GHS Ismaila, Swabi). Minor spelling of names may differ from the print.

decorative: Unit opener illustration of the pyramids of Egypt with palm trees and a camel.
issues: The skills list repeats "use an organogram to demonstrate the different aspects of the Egyptian people" twice in the book; it appears once here.

decorative: Picture chart "Footprints of Human History" with small pictures for each period (cave dwellers, a bronze chariot, pyramids, a mosque skyline, Mohenjo-daro ruins and a priest-king statue, battle scenes, a moon astronaut).
issues: The chart dates are approximate. The Stone Age began far earlier than 35000 BC (about 3.3 million years ago); 35000 BC marks the late Palaeolithic. The Indus Valley mature phase is usually dated about 2600–1900 BC. Recorded as printed.
"stuents" is misspelled in the teachers' note. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph of the UN headquarters building in New York with flags, captioned: "At the end of World War II, the United Nations Organization (UNO) was founded on October 24, 1945, United States".
issues: The UN Charter lists six principal organs; the sixth, the Trusteeship Council, suspended operations in 1994, which is why many books now list five. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Pompeii-styled artefact" (a bronze jug), "1652 Massachusetts Bay Colony shilling" (a silver coin with a tree) and "Original written texts" (a hand writing with a quill).
issues: "all the time preceding human existence till the invention of writing" is odd; prehistory is the time of human existence before writing. Recorded as printed.
The Neolithic is usually called the "New Stone Age"; "late Stone Age" is a different term in African archaeology. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Illustration of a river-valley settlement (palm trees, mud houses, farmers ploughing with oxen, people carrying water, an irrigation channel) with seven empty label boxes for students to fill in.
issues: "Mesopotmia" is misspelled in the text. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Map captioned "Mesopotamian Civilizations": the Fertile Crescent shaded pink from Upper and Lower Egypt along the Nile, through Phoenicia, to Assyria and Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates; Anatolia, Media, the Syrian Desert, Sinai, the Mediterranean Sea and the Persian Sea labelled.
Photographs captioned "Masopotamia today (Central Bank of Iraq)" (a modern twisted glass tower) and "Sultan Ahmet Masjid in present day Turkey (Blue Mosque)".
Photograph captioned "Metallurgical works": ancient bronze tools, ornaments and vessels.
issues: The caption misspells "Masopotamia". The Blue Mosque is in Istanbul, which lies outside historic Mesopotamia; the photo illustrates present-day Turkey. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Map titled "The Earliest Civilizations" (scale 0–400 miles): Sumer from 3200 B.C. (Kish, Nippur, Lagash, Uruk, Ur, Eridu) shaded pink — Dynasty of Kish c. 2800, Dynasty I of Ur c. 2500, Dynasty of Lagash c. 2500–2360; the Akkadian Empire 2350–2300 (with campaigns of Sargon I) shaded teal from the Persian Gulf to Ashur, Nineveh, Mari and Tall Halaf; Egypt Old Kingdom 2850–2052 along the Nile (Gizeh, Memphis, Heliopolis, Tanis, Thebes, Abu Simbel); Byblos, Tyre, Jericho, Elam and Susa.
issues: "Sumerain" is misspelled in the text. Sumer flourished from about 4500–1900 BC; "6000 years ago" is approximate. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Seals" (a cylinder seal and its clay impression), "Cuneiform, Sumerian writing" (a clay tablet), "Sail boat were invented for faster sailing" (a reed boat model with a sail), "Chariot was used in ancient racing and warfare" (a model of an ox-drawn chariot) and "Sumerians earthenware and tools" (pots, axes, mace-heads and sickles).
issues: Painted pottery and porcelain are not Sumerian inventions "still in use"; porcelain was developed much later in China. Recorded as printed.
The caption "Sail boat were invented" should read "Sail boats were invented". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Sumerian Queen": a stone statue of a seated woman in a fleece robe.
Photograph of the ruins of a ziggurat.
Painting captioned "Hanging Gardens of Babylon": stepped terraces planted with palms and trees.
issues: Hammurabi was the sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon, not its first king (he began his reign about 1792 BC). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Hammurabi code in cuneiform script": the top of the basalt stele showing Hammurabi before the god Shamash, surrounded by cuneiform.
Photograph captioned "Mosque-Madrasa of Sultan Hassan Salah-Din Square, Modern day Egypt".
issues: Even in Hammurabi's own code, punishments differed by social class; the claim that unequal laws began only after his death and caused the decline is a simplification. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "An Egyptian sculpture": a pale seated stone figure.
Photograph captioned "King Sahure": a dark stone statue of a seated king beside a smaller figure.
issues: Egypt is bordered by (not surrounded by) the two seas, and the closing quotation mark after "the gift of the Nile" is missing. Recorded as printed.
The pyramids were built in the Old Kingdom, after the predynastic period, not during it. Recorded as printed.
Sneferu, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure were pharaohs; the pyramids are named after them. Sneferu's pyramids are at Dahshur and Meidum, not Giza. Recorded as printed.
Hatshepsut ruled in the New Kingdom (18th dynasty), not the Old Kingdom where this box is placed. Recorded as printed.
The Middle Kingdom lasted c. 2050–1650 BC; "1170 BC" overlaps the New Kingdom given on the next page. Chariots reached Egypt with the Hyksos, after the Middle Kingdom. Recorded as printed.
Sahure was an Old Kingdom (5th dynasty) king, though the photo sits beside the Middle Kingdom text. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Tomb painting captioned "Early Pharaohs": a pharaoh in a white crown and robe facing a figure in a leopard skin.
Tomb painting: a farmer ploughing with a spotted ox while a woman sows seed; a row of trees below.
issues: Nefertiti is generally known as a queen (royal wife of Akhenaten), not certainly a pharaoh. Cleopatra VII ruled in the Ptolemaic period (51–30 BC), long after the New Kingdom. Recorded as printed.
The battle of Actium was in 31 BC; Egypt became a Roman province in 30 BC after Cleopatra's death. Recorded as printed.
"Cattle … together with ducks, cows, and geese" repeats cattle/cows. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Paintings captioned "Shaduf, a Traditional System of Irrigation;" (a man working a pole-and-bucket lever beside a well) and "Ancient Granaries" (a mud-brick wall honeycombed with arched storage chambers).
Tomb painting: four figures in white linen garments, with hieroglyphs above.
Tomb painting in two rows showing craftsmen at work with tools.

Photograph of a limestone fragment carved with columns of hieroglyphs (birds, eyes, a snake), captioned: "This limestone block fragment came from the debris of the north wall of the antechamber within the pyramid of King Pepy-I at Saqqara."
Photographs captioned "Mummified body of Tutankhamen" and "Gold Funerary mask of Tutankhamen".
issues: Writing predates the pyramids (the first pyramid was built c. 2650 BC), so writing "around 3000 BC … in pyramids" is inaccurate. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "The Great Pyramid of Giza": three pyramids at dusk with camels in the foreground.
Photograph captioned "The Abu Simbel Temple of Ramses II in Egypt": four colossal seated statues carved into a cliff.
issues: Abu Simbel is a rock-cut temple, not a pyramid, though it appears under "The Pyramids". Recorded as printed.
"Pharoahs" is misspelled (Pharaohs). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Pharaoh as King": a stone statue of a pharaoh wearing a tall crown, arms crossed.
issues: "Next to him" should be "next to them" (the pharaohs); "This strata" should be "this stratum"; and the text says first that all officials reported to the vizier, then that priests and others reported to the Pharaoh. Recorded as printed.
"Paharohs" is misspelled (Pharaohs). Recorded as printed.
MCQ iv is ambiguous: the text gives rights and power to women in both Egypt (p. 12) and Sumer (p. 10). "Eygpt" is misspelled. The answer follows the stronger statement (Egypt).
MCQ v has two correct options (Euphrates and Tigris), and "Euprates" is misspelled.
The sixth MCQ is unnumbered in the book, and "Antalia" presumably means Anatolia.
The heading misspells "Eygypt". Recorded as Egypt in the transcription.
"Chariots" is listed twice in Egypt's advances, and "Flat mud plains" offered Mesopotamia no natural defence (the opposite is the usual point). Recorded as printed.
"Eygypt" is misspelled in question iv. Recorded as printed.
"Chronologist" is defined as the science (chronology) rather than a person who studies it; ziggurats were temple platforms, not usually "capped by a tomb". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Unit opener photograph of four ancient Chinese bronze ritual vessels with lids and handles.
issues: "Mehergarh" is usually spelled Mehrgarh. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Portrait captioned "King Wu": a bearded ruler in a tall ornate crown and dark-collared robe.
issues: "Huang Ye" should read Huang He (the Yellow River). Recorded as printed.

The Xia dynasty is traditionally dated c. 2070–1600 BC (about 470 years), not 1100 years; Jie was only its last ruler, not ruler for the whole period. The text also dates Tang's victory to 1650 BC but the Shang start to 1600 BC. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Bronze wares were recognized as a sign of power": a chart of Shang bronze vessel types (tripods, wine cups, cauldrons) and a large bronze bell decorated with a face.
issues: "strengthen" should be "strengthens". Recorded as printed.
Most of the Grand Canal was built much later, under the Sui dynasty (AD 581–618); only early sections date from the late Zhou period. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Illustration captioned "Small villages and towns were ruled by local lords who were loyal to the emperor": a walled village with a watchtower, terraced green hills, flooded rice paddies and a canal.
Pictures captioned "Horse drawn Chariot" (a two-horse chariot with a spoked wheel), "Oracle bone script" (a turtle shell inscribed with early characters) and "Chopsticks".
issues: "valubale" is misspelled (valuable). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Temple where Confucius taught his students" (bronze statues of Confucius and seated pupils before a red-walled temple) and "A ceremony honoring Confucius on 28th September in China. It is an official holiday in Taiwan, known as Teachers' Day." (performers in pink robes in a temple courtyard).
issues: "hilighted" is misspelled (highlighted). Recorded as printed.
This saying is popularly attributed to Confucius, but its closest classical source is the philosopher Xunzi. Recorded as printed.
The note refers to a map of Pakistan, but none is printed on this page; a map has been added above for the activity.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Town Planning in Mehrgarh": excavated mud-brick walls forming a grid of rectangular rooms.
Photographs captioned "Pottery and Bead Making at Mehrgarh": rows of lapis-blue and stone beads beside a scale bar, and two glowing painted pots decorated with humped bulls.
issues: "visuals details" should be "visual details". Recorded as printed.
Copper/bronze objects belong to Mehrgarh's later phases (after c. 5500 BC), not its earliest Neolithic period. Recorded as printed.
"Pottrey" is misspelled (Pottery), and "(1942)" means Catherine Jarrige was born in 1942. Recorded as printed.
The note spells the site both "Mehergarh" and "Mehrgarh". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Indus bearded Priest King Statue found in Mohenjo Daro in 1927": a steatite bust of a bearded man wearing a trefoil-patterned robe.
Photographs of six square Indus seals engraved with animals (a unicorn-like bull, a zebu) and script signs.
issues: Because the Indus script is undeciphered, no written laws are known; statements about specific laws (nature, violence, taxes, respect for women) are interpretations, not established facts. Recorded as printed.
The "Priest King" was found at Mohenjo-daro in the 1925–26 excavation season, usually dated 1925–27; the 1927 date is accepted with caution. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Brick and rammed Earth homes and streets of Harappa": excavated brick walls, a drain line and a round brick well.
Photograph captioned "Public Bath": the brick-lined Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro with steps leading down into it.
issues: Most houses at Mohenjo-daro and Harappa were built of standard baked (kiln-fired) bricks; sun-dried mud bricks were used mainly for foundations and fill. Recorded as printed.
The Great Bath stood on the raised citadel mound in the west of Mohenjo-daro; it was sealed with bitumen (natural tar) and gypsum plaster. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Granary": rows of parallel brick platforms of the Harappa granary.
issues: Ranking Indus social conditions above Babylon and Egypt, and the four-class division, are speculative, since the script is undeciphered. Recorded as printed.

The "unburied skeletons" were later shown to come from different periods, not one massacre, and some copper/bronze weapons (spearheads, arrowheads, daggers) have been found at Indus sites, so "no weapons were found" is inaccurate. Recorded as printed.

The right-hand column gives clues rather than answers: row iii shows evidence, not a hypothesis, and row iv states an unknown rather than the information needed. The book's closing bracket in row iv is missing. Recorded as printed.

Two summary points are not supported by the unit's text: nothing in the chapter says King Tang "showed no mercy" to rule-breakers, and no parallels between Indus rulers and Hammurabi or Ramses are discussed (Indus rulers are unknown). Recorded as printed.
"Mehergarh" is spelled differently from "Mehrgarh" in the lesson. Recorded as printed.
"civilazation" is misspelled in question 3 I. Recorded as printed.
The Mohenjo-daro houses were mostly of baked bricks, and some weapons have in fact been found at Indus sites (see the lesson notes). The matching follows the book.
"more than one gods" should be "more than one god". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Unit opener photograph of the columns of a ruined Greco-Roman temple on a hill under a blue sky.
Photograph captioned "Modern day Tehran reflects the cultural heritage and beauty of the golden age of the Persian Empire": the Tehran skyline.
issues: "one of the benevolent empire" should read "one of the benevolent empires". The full list of lands describes the Achaemenid Empire at its height (c. 500 BC), not every Persian dynasty up to the 20th century. Recorded as printed.
559–530 BC are the dates of Cyrus's reign, not of his "arrival". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Pictures captioned "Cyrus the Great" (a profile portrait of a bearded king in a helmet-crown) and "Darius the Great" (a weathered stone relief of a winged figure).
issues: Timeline errors, recorded as printed: (1) Cyrus died in 530 BC fighting the Massagetae in Central Asia, not after invading India; (2) Cambyses was Cyrus's son and died in 522 BC, when Darius seized the throne from Bardiya (Smerdis), so the entry dated 521 BC is slightly late; (3) Xerxes I ruled 486–465 BC, not within 385–359 BC; (4) the Darius defeated by Alexander was Darius III, not Darius the Great.
Assyria had already fallen (612 BC) to the Medes and Babylonians before Cyrus; he conquered the Medes, Lydia and Babylonia (which then held Phoenicia). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Depiction of an Achaemenid queen and daughter of Cyrus the Great / Photo by A. Davey, National Museum of Iran" (a carved blue stone head) and "Central medallion of a Qashqai rug, 19th century. Persian hand-woven rugs and carpets were noted for their beautiful designs and vibrant colours".
issues: Zoroastrianism is usually described as monotheistic in its worship of Ahura Mazda, though it also has dualist elements; the wording "Persian's society" should be "Persian society". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Iran, Shiraz, Cyrus Palace, 2500 BC" (rows of broken stone columns on a plain) and "Tomb of Cyrus in Pasargadae, Iran, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2015)" (a gabled stone tomb on a stepped plinth).
Photographs of Persian jewellery (a jewelled serpent bangle and a bead necklace) and a gold bowl, captioned "The Persian gold bowl with imagery of lions".
issues: Cyrus's palace at Pasargadae dates from about 550 BC, not 2500 BC, and lies about 90 km north-east of Shiraz. Pasargadae became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004, not 2015. Recorded as printed.
The box is headed "Cyrus Palace" but describes Persepolis, a different site built by Darius I. Recorded as printed.

It was Darius I (the Great), not Darius III, who introduced the single coinage (the daric) and standard weights and measures. The Silk Road developed later, under the Chinese Han dynasty (2nd century BC). Recorded as printed.
The jewellery caption is blurred in the scan; it appears to read "Persian glass and precious stones jewellery".
The first half of this note is blurred in the scan; the wording above is reconstructed from the legible part.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Ruins in Taxila": a grass-covered stone stupa mound.
Mosaic captioned "The battle of Isuss between Alexander and Darius III in 333 BC resulted in the ultimate fall of the Persian Empire.": horsemen and spears in battle.
issues: Alexander's invasion of the Persian Empire began in 334 BC; by 330 BC the Achaemenid dynasty had fallen. Recorded as printed.
"Isuss" is misspelled (Issus). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Greek Monuments": the Acropolis of Athens lit at dusk, with the Parthenon on top.
issues: Solon's reforms are usually dated 594 BC. Recorded as printed.
"ancient Greek" should read "ancient Greece". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "The Parthenon, as shown below, was the temple on top of a hill in the center of the city.": the columned Parthenon against a blue sky.
Photograph of a marble bust of Socrates.
Photograph captioned "Ruins of Sparta": low stone foundations in a green valley below mountains.
issues: Not all Athenian officials were chosen by lot — the ten generals (strategoi) were elected by vote. Only adult male citizens could vote; women, slaves and foreigners could not. Recorded as printed.
The caption says "as shown below" although the photo is beside the text. Recorded as printed.

The Spartan assembly (Apella) included all adult male Spartan citizens rather than "elected Spartans"; the classes are usually given as Spartiates (citizens), perioikoi (free non-citizens who were craftsmen and traders) and helots (state-owned serfs). Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Ancient Theater - The Theater at Epidaurus is built into a hillside.": a semicircular stone theatre with tiers of seats.
Diagram of an Archimedean screw — "coil rotates and lifts water" — raising water from a channel; photograph captioned "Ancient Greek Vase" (a black-figure amphora with handles).
issues: Eratosthenes' figure (about 250,000 stadia) is usually converted to roughly 24,000–29,000 miles, so his estimate was close to the true value. The panel's wording "The Ptolemy's view" is ungrammatical. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Statue of Alexander in armour, with the caption heading "Alexander's takeover of Egypt".
issues: Alexander's empire was among the largest of the ancient world, but not "the largest the world has ever witnessed" — the Mongol and British empires were far larger. Recorded as printed.
Hellas was the Greeks' name for their land; they called themselves Hellenes. Recorded as printed.
Alexander entered the Punjab and fought Porus at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) in 326 BC; 327 BC is when his campaign into the Indus region began. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Painting of the battle of Alexander and Porus: war elephants with howdahs charging Macedonian soldiers with round shields.

Photograph captioned "Ruins of Sirkap in Taxila" with the note "Sirkap is the only Greek city in Taxila. Sirkap was once a thriving ancient metropolis, complete with streets, houses, shops and places of worship.": low dry-stone walls and a domed stupa in a green field.
Photograph captioned "Alexander's monument in Jhelum. This monument is a large white marble structure with 16 arches built in a blend of Greek architecture.": a modern white building with columns.
issues: Ancient sources describe the Battle of the Hydaspes (326 BC) as a victory for Alexander, after which he restored Porus as a ruler under him; "indecisive" is the book's interpretation. Recorded as printed.
Ancient sources place Nicaea and Bucephala on opposite banks of the Jhelum (Hydaspes), not both on the left bank. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Heritage Museum / Lok Virsa Museum, Islamabad.": museum displays of Gandhara relics, a seated Buddha figure and a craftsman diorama.
issues: The Roman Empire (27 BC – AD 476 in the West) belongs to Classical Antiquity, not the Middle Ages, which began after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Recorded as printed.
"Lok Versa" should read Lok Virsa. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Painting captioned "Market Life in Roman Empire": a busy Roman market street with stalls and shoppers.
Painting captioned "Roman Assembly": senators in white togas seated in a curved hall while one speaks.

Map titled "The Spread of Christianity in the Roman Empire by the Second and Fourth Centuries": shading shows areas reached by about AD 185 and by the time of Constantine (AD 325) — Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt and North Africa around the eastern Mediterranean most strongly, then Italy, Spain, France (Gaul), the Balkans and Britain.
issues: This box places the Middle Ages after the fall of Rome, which contradicts the previous page's statement that the Roman Empire rose "during the Middle Ages". The Middle Ages are often dated to the 15th century. Recorded as printed.

The Romans developed and spread these inventions but did not invent all of them: arches, aqueducts, drains, roads and grid-planned cities existed earlier (e.g. Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley, Greece). The map shows spread up to AD 325, not AD 600. Recorded as printed.
The Median army's switch to Cyrus is usually dated 550 BC; "Medean" should be "Median". The fall of Rome is not discussed in the unit text. Recorded as printed.
MCQ iv has no exactly correct option: the Susa–Sardis route was the Royal Road, which is not literally an early Silk Road. The answer follows the closest option.
The unit text never mentions the pope, so this question goes beyond the chapter. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Unit opener photograph of an ancient stone fort with high walls and towers.
issues: "Nada Kings" should read Nanda Kings. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Buddha Statue": a giant seated bronze Buddha among trees.
issues: The book spells the castes inconsistently (Kshatryas / Kashtriyas, Vaishyas / Vaisyas, Shudras / Sudra) and the chart misspells "Untochables". Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Gautama Buddha": a richly carved temple facade with a seated Buddha in a central niche.
issues: Jains do not believe in a creator god but do revere the liberated souls (Tirthankaras), so "does not believe in any divinity" is a simplification. The five Jain vows are non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, chastity and non-possession. Recorded as printed.

The box is titled "Gandhara Civilization" but opens with a sentence repeated from the previous page about the Aryans. Buddhism began in the Ganges region (Bihar); Gandhara became a major centre of Buddhism later. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "This picture shows Stupa at Sanchi, India. It was built by Ashoka. The Stupa believed to store the ashes of Buddha.": a large hemispherical stone stupa with a railing, among trees.
issues: 321–185 BCE are the dates of the whole Mauryan dynasty; Chandragupta founded it around 321 BCE and ruled until about 297 BCE. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Postage stamp captioned "A commemorative postage stamp on the emperor Chandragupta Mauria, issued by Indian government in 2001.": a gold-toned stamp showing the seated emperor.
Photograph captioned "Unified Currency of Mauryan Empire": two worn copper coins, one showing an elephant.
issues: "Mauria" in the caption should read Maurya. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Portrait captioned "Ashoka, the Mauryan Emperor": a turbaned ruler in jewelled dress.
Photograph of the lion capital on top of an Ashokan pillar.
issues: 304–232 BC are Ashoka's dates of birth and death; he reigned c. 268–232 BC. The turning point in his eighth year was the bloody Kalinga war, after which he gave up conquest. His policy is usually called "conquest by dharma (righteousness)". Recorded as printed.
The figure of 84,000 stupas comes from Buddhist legend rather than historical evidence. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Sculpture of Kanishka": a carved stone head with curly hair.
issues: Kanishka is usually counted as the fourth Kushan emperor, after Kujula Kadphises, Vima Takto and Vima Kadphises. Recorded as printed.
Kanishka was a great patron of Gandhara art, but the school developed over a long period and was not "established" by one ruler. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photographs captioned "Kushan's Gold coins": two gold coins, one with a crowned king and one with a standing deity.

Photographs captioned "Kanishka was identified as the builder of massive ancient forts. Takht-i-Bahi, also known as Monastery of Kanishka. It is well preserved in Mardan." (hillside ruins of a monastery) and "The Qila Mubarak fort at Bathinda — Kanishka was identified as the builder of massive ancient forts." (a large brick fort).
issues: Buddhism is usually said to have reached China in the 1st century CE (under the Han emperor Ming), slightly earlier than stated. Recorded as printed.

Takht-i-Bahi is a Buddhist monastery, not a fort, and its link to Kanishka is traditional rather than proven; the claim that Kanishka built Qila Mubarak at Bathinda is likewise local tradition. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "The Ajanta and Ellora caves are carved into mountainside in present day India. Both sites are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.": the rock-cut Kailasa temple at Ellora seen from above.
issues: The paragraph contradicts itself: it first says Ajanta's caves are all Buddhist, then that Ajanta's art is themed around Buddhism and Jainism. The monsoon-retreat description is usually given for Ajanta, not Ellora. Ellora's many Hindu and Jain caves also mean "masterpieces of Buddhist religious art" applies fully only to Ajanta. Recorded as printed.
The Gupta era began in AD 320, which falls in the third decade of the 4th century rather than the second. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "A Coin of Gupta Period": a gold coin showing a king on horseback.
issues: The first point is inaccurate: the Indus civilization flourished c. 2600–1900 BC, while the Aryans arrived later (c. 1500 BC, as the unit itself says). Recorded as printed.
"Chosse" in the heading should read "Choose". Recorded as printed.
Several options are misspelled in the book: "Kansihka" (Kanishka), "Janism" (Jainism), "Budhism" (Buddhism), "Parshapur" (Purushapur), "Magdh" (Magadha).

decorative: Unit opener photograph of a minaret silhouetted against an orange sunset sky.
issues: "comapre" is misspelled (compare). "UN charter of Human Rights" most likely refers to the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). Recorded as printed.

The chart places Hazrat Zikriya between Hazrat Sulaiman and Hazrat Yahya; in this simplified drawing Zikriya is omitted for space and is listed in the caption. The book's chart is a sequence of famous prophets, not an exact family tree.

decorative: Photograph captioned "The cave Hira in the mountain Jabal al-Nour where, Hazrat Muhammad Rasulullah Khatam-un-Nabiyeen (ﷺ) received his first revelation from the angel Gabriel.": the rocky mouth of the cave with a marked plaque.
issues: The birth year is commonly given as AD 570 or 571. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Photograph captioned "Masjid e Nabwi in Madinah Munawwara": the mosque with its green dome and tall minarets above a crowded marble courtyard.
issues: Scholars usually divide the Charter of Madinah into 47 or 52 clauses; the figure of 63 depends on how the text is divided. Recorded as printed.

This paragraph judges a whole community in general terms; historians refer to the breaking of the Charter by particular Jewish tribes of Madinah (Banu Qaynuqa, Banu Nadir, Banu Qurayza). Recorded as printed.
Hazrat Abu Bakr (رضی اللہ عنہ) ruled for about 2 years and 3 months (AH 11–13). The AH column gives the year each caliphate began. Recorded as printed.

decorative: The book's map also includes an inset "Spread of Islam in Southeast Asia" (13th/14th, 15th and 16th centuries), showing Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula, Java, Borneo, Brunei, Celebes and Mindanao, and arrows "to Indonesia" from India.
issues: The main Persian armies were defeated by AD 642 (Nahavand), about ten years after AD 632, but the conquest of all Persia was completed around AD 651. Egypt's conquest was completed by AD 641–642. Recorded as printed.

decorative: Calligraphy medallion of the name "Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (رضی اللہ عنہ)" in gold on green.
Photograph captioned "Masjid Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (رضی اللہ عنہ) in Doha, Qatar.": a domed mosque with arched arcades and a tall minaret.
issues: Iraq and Syria were only partly under Muslim control by Hazrat Abu Bakr's death in AD 634; their provincial organisation belongs mainly to Hazrat Umar's caliphate. Recorded as printed.
